standard.title: Regional and global government roles
standard.description: the Australian Government's role and responsibilities at a regional and global level
standard.prior_knowledge: Students know how individuals and groups participate in civic life in Australia and contribute to global citizenship (AC9HC9K05). They understand legislative processes shaping government policy (AC9HC9K02).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the Australian Government's role and responsibilities at a regional and global level, analysing and evaluating its participation in relation to a global issue.

nodes.label: Forms of regional and global participation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the main ways Australia contributes to and participates in the Asia-Pacific region and globally, including membership of international organisations and agreements.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three specific forms of Australia's regional or global participation (e.g. peacekeeping, development aid, UN involvement) with brief descriptions of each.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the full range of ways Australia participates in the Asia-Pacific region and globally — exchange programs, peacekeeping, election monitoring, development aid, health programs, disaster management, and international treaty participation including the UN Security Council — using accurate examples.
wider: Investigate Australia's participation in a specific multilateral body (e.g. UN Security Council, G20) and evaluate what membership requires and delivers
Research how Australia's engagement with the Asia-Pacific has changed over time and what this reveals about shifting foreign policy priorities
Examine how Australia's international development commitments compare with those of comparable nations (e.g. aid spending as percentage of GNI)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have only vague knowledge of participation forms cannot complete the evaluative analysis in subsequent nodes — they lack the factual base to assess effectiveness or compare responses.

response_modes.reason: Build a concrete repertoire of participation types and examples before moving to evaluation. Students should be able to name specific programs or agreements, not just categories.

success_criteria: Names at least three distinct forms of Australia's regional or global participation
Provides a specific example for at least two of those forms
Distinguishes between regional (Asia-Pacific) and global participation

nodes.label: International treaty obligations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain Australia's responsibilities and commitments under key international treaties and conventions, using specific examples.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain Australia's responsibilities under at least one international treaty or convention, identifying what the commitment requires of the Australian Government.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate Australia's responsibilities under two or more international treaties or conventions (e.g. UN Sustainable Development Agenda, UNFCCC, Refugee Convention, UNDRIP) and explain how each shapes Australian law or government policy.
wider: Examine how the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples has shaped (or not shaped) Australian policy toward First Nations Australians
Compare the binding vs advisory nature of different international instruments and what this means for Australia's obligations
Investigate a case where Australia has been criticised for failing to meet its international obligations and analyse the government's response
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding treaty obligations is prerequisite to evaluating Australia's participation — students cannot assess effectiveness without knowing what commitments Australia has made. This directly feeds AC9HC10K04 as well.

response_modes.reason: Students often conflate signing, ratifying and implementing treaties, or assume all international agreements are equally binding. Invest in clarifying the legal status and practical requirements of different instruments.
The UNDRIP direction is particularly rich — it connects treaty obligations to First Nations Australians' lived experience and to the descriptor's explicit inclusion of First Nations contexts.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The UNDRIP and Paris Agreement directions are substantive enrichment contexts that connect abstract treaty obligations to concrete Australian policy debates, giving students materials for genuine evaluative argument.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one specific treaty or convention and explains what it requires of Australia
Explains how the treaty has shaped at least one aspect of Australian law or government policy
Distinguishes between Australia's commitments and its actions in at least one case

nodes.label: Analysing and evaluating global participation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse and evaluate the reasons for and effectiveness of Australia's participation in the region and globally with regard to a specific global issue.
nodes.minimum_width: Analyse Australia's participation in relation to one global issue, identifying reasons for involvement and offering a supported judgement about its effectiveness.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse and evaluate the reasons for and effectiveness of Australia's participation in the region or globally with regard to a significant global issue (e.g. human rights, climate, conflict, democratic challenges), including consideration of competing perspectives and evidence.
wider: Compare the responses of different governments and organisations to the same global issue and evaluate why responses differ
Investigate how global interconnectedness both creates and helps solve the issue being studied
Evaluate the impact of the issue on First Nations Australians' reconciliation, truth-telling and sovereignty alongside its broader impact on Australian identity

response_modes.reason: Evaluation requires students to weigh evidence and acknowledge competing views. Support students in distinguishing description of actions from evaluation of effectiveness — these are different claims requiring different evidence.
Widening the issue context (e.g. examining climate plus human rights rather than one alone) gives students comparative material for more nuanced evaluation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The comparative responses direction and the First Nations sovereignty direction are each independently rich — comparing national responses reveals why participation choices are made, while the First Nations direction connects global policy to domestic equity in a substantive way.
success_criteria: Analyses at least two reasons for Australia's participation in relation to a named global issue
Provides a supported evaluative judgement about the effectiveness of that participation
Acknowledges at least one limitation or competing perspective in the evaluation

nodes.label: Global interconnectedness and Australia's choices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how global interconnectedness affects Australia's capacity to address global issues, and evaluate how this shapes Australian identity and policy choices.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how global interconnectedness has either helped or hindered Australia's ability to respond to a global issue.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain how the forces of global interconnectedness both exacerbate and enhance Australia's ability to address a key global issue, and evaluate impacts on Australia's identity and citizens' choices to act in the global interest.
wider: Investigate a specific case where Australia's international trade relationships have created tensions with its stated commitment to human rights
Examine how diaspora communities in Australia influence Australian foreign policy choices in relation to their countries of origin
Evaluate how the concept of global citizenship has evolved and what it demands of Australian citizens specifically

response_modes.reason: This node brings together participation knowledge, treaty obligations, and evaluative reasoning into a reflective account of Australia's global position and identity. Teaching investment is in supporting synthesis rather than adding factual content.

success_criteria: Explains at least one way global interconnectedness enables and one way it constrains Australia's response to a global issue
Connects Australia's global participation to its national identity or values
Evaluates the implications for citizens acting in the global interest
